scenes.tts: A small, steady input arrives at one point on a dendrite. How much of it survives the trip along the branch?
scenes.visual: A long thin dendrite drawn across the screen, with an electrode at its left end. The question appears above.
scenes.narration: A small, steady input arrives at one point on a dendrite. How much of it survives the trip along the branch?

scenes.tts: A dendrite is a thin tube of salty cytoplasm, wrapped in leaky membrane.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of the dendrite: salty core inside, membrane with small leak channels in the wall.
scenes.narration: A dendrite is a thin tube of salty cytoplasm, wrapped in leaky membrane.

scenes.tts: Current injected at one point has two paths. It can flow along the core, or out through the membrane.
scenes.visual: Teal current arrows enter at the left; some run along the core, some exit through the wall. Labels: core (axial) path, membrane path.
scenes.narration: Current injected at one point has two paths. It can flow along the core, or out through the membrane.

scenes.tts: Think of a garden hose full of small holes. Some water leaks out at every hole.
scenes.visual: The dendrite morphs into a garden hose with pinholes; water sprays out of each hole.
scenes.narration: Think of a garden hose full of small holes. Some water leaks out at every hole.

scenes.tts: So the farther along you go, the less is left.
scenes.visual: The water stream inside the hose thins from left to right.
scenes.narration: So the farther along you go, the less is left.

scenes.tts: How far the current gets depends on which path is easier. A wide core carries it farther. A tight wall loses less.
scenes.visual: Split screen: a wide core with arrows reaching far; a tight wall with few holes and arrows reaching far.
scenes.narration: How far the current gets depends on which path is easier. A wide core carries it farther. A tight wall loses less.

scenes.tts: The length constant puts that contest into one number.
scenes.visual: Title card: length constant, λ.
scenes.narration: The length constant puts that contest into one number.

scenes.tts: It is the length of cable whose core resistance equals the resistance of its own membrane.
scenes.visual: A segment of length λ is highlighted. Two resistor icons: core resistance along it, membrane resistance through its wall, with an equals sign between.
scenes.narration: It is the length of cable whose core resistance equals the resistance of its own membrane.

scenes.tts: Along a long, uniform cable, a steady signal falls exponentially with distance.
scenes.visual: A plot of steady V against distance x: an exponential decay from V0. On screen: V(x) = V0 × e^(−x/λ), λ = √(rm / ri).
scenes.narration: Along a long, uniform cable, a steady signal falls exponentially with distance.

scenes.tts: So, one length constant away from the source, is the signal gone?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. At x = λ, is the steady signal gone?
scenes.narration: So, one length constant away from the source, is the signal gone?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: No. About thirty-seven percent remains. Smaller, not gone.
scenes.caption: No. About 37% remains. Smaller, not gone.
scenes.visual: A marker at x = λ on the decay curve reads 37% of V0. On screen only: e^−1 ≈ 0.37; at 2λ, 0.135.
scenes.narration: No. About 37% remains. Smaller, not gone.

scenes.tts: Two length constants away, about fourteen percent remains. The signal keeps shrinking, but it never simply stops.
scenes.caption: Two length constants away, about 14% remains. The signal keeps shrinking, but it never simply stops.
scenes.visual: The marker moves to x = 2λ and reads about 14% of V0.
scenes.narration: Two length constants away, about 14% remains. The signal keeps shrinking, but it never simply stops.

scenes.tts: Here is the lesson's worked example. Watch the steady signal shrink at each length constant along the cable.
scenes.visual: Worked problem, part 4, on screen only: λ = 0.5 mm, −10 mV held at the source; −3.68 mV at 0.5 mm; −1.35 mV at 1 mm. Each value lights up on the decay curve in turn.
scenes.narration: Here is the lesson's worked example. Watch the steady signal shrink at each length constant along the cable.

scenes.tts: The length constant sets the scale of the decay. It is not a cutoff.
scenes.visual: The ΔV curve continues past λ and 2λ, approaching zero from below for the −10 mV example but never reaching it. Label: λ is a scale, not a cutoff.
scenes.narration: The length constant sets the scale of the decay. It is not a cutoff.

scenes.tts: A leakier membrane shortens it. So does a narrower core.
scenes.visual: Slider-style comparison, mirroring the CableLengthConstant simulation: a leakier membrane pulls the 37% point toward the source; a narrower core does the same.
scenes.narration: A leakier membrane shortens it. So does a narrower core.

scenes.tts: Try it in the lesson's simulation. Make the membrane leakier, and watch the thirty-seven percent point move toward the source.
scenes.caption: Try it in the lesson's simulation. Make the membrane leakier, and watch the 37% point move toward the source.
scenes.visual: A mock-up of the CableLengthConstant simulation: a leak slider moves up and the 37% cursor slides toward the held end.
scenes.narration: Try it in the lesson's simulation. Make the membrane leakier, and watch the 37% point move toward the source.

scenes.tts: With the same membrane and cytoplasm, the length constant grows as the square root of the diameter.
scenes.visual: A wider cable: the 37% point moves away from the source. On screen: λ ∝ √diameter.
scenes.narration: With the same membrane and cytoplasm, the length constant grows as the square root of the diameter.

scenes.tts: Capacitance does not change the shape. It only sets how fast the steady state arrives.
scenes.visual: The steady decay curve stays fixed while a growing curve fills in under it, faster or slower. Label: C sets speed, not shape.
scenes.narration: Capacitance does not change the shape. It only sets how fast the steady state arrives.

scenes.tts: Now double the leak, with everything else the same.
scenes.visual: A table builds on screen: before, leak doubled. Row 1: total leak (compact cell) 10 nS, 20 nS.
scenes.narration: Now double the leak, with everything else the same.

scenes.tts: In a compact cell, input resistance halves. The same current gives half the change.
scenes.visual: Rows appear: input resistance 100 → 50 MΩ; steady change for −100 pA, −10 → −5 mV.
scenes.narration: In a compact cell, input resistance halves. The same current gives half the change.

scenes.tts: The time constant halves too, so the voltage gets there sooner.
scenes.visual: Row appears: time constant 20 → 10 ms. Two charging curves overlay, the new one smaller and faster.
scenes.narration: The time constant halves too, so the voltage gets there sooner.

scenes.tts: And along the cable, the length constant shrinks. Signals reach less far.
scenes.visual: Row appears: length constant 0.5 → 0.354 mm. The decay curve steepens.
scenes.narration: And along the cable, the length constant shrinks. Signals reach less far.

scenes.tts: Does the passive balance point move? That depends on the added leak's reversal potential. With no applied current, and the pump's own current set aside, doubling every leak in proportion leaves it unchanged.
scenes.visual: The voltage scale returns: both ropes thicken together and the marker does not move. Small label: no applied current; pump's direct current omitted.
scenes.narration: Does the passive balance point move? That depends on the added leak's reversal potential. With no applied current, and the pump's own current set aside, doubling every leak in proportion leaves it unchanged.

scenes.tts: More leak makes a cell faster. But its responses are smaller, and they reach less far.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: more leak = faster, smaller, more local.
scenes.narration: More leak makes a cell faster. But its responses are smaller, and they reach less far.
